newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada unemployment surges in September.
newsitem.headline: Canada unemployment surges in September.

text.p: Canadian unemployment on Friday jumped to an unexpectedly high 9.9 percent in September, putting Canada's economic recovery in doubt and prompting calls for more interest rate cuts from the Bank of Canada.

"This is disappointingly week," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "If you look at the elements of the report, all (the job losses) are pretty much in business services and this suggests to me that domestic demand remains pretty weak.
Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said the surge in unemployment from 9.4 percent in August was disappointing but that monthly jobs reports were "volatile."
"There is no doubt that the figures are disappointing. However, we mustn't lose sight of the fact that the monthly data are volatile," Martin told Parliament.

Statistics Canada, a government agency, said full-time employment fell by 86,000, wiping out the 72,000-job gain in August and cutting the year's total gains in half. Part-time employment rose by 39,000 in September.
Three-quarters of the overall job decline occurred in Ontario, Canada's richest province. Seven of Canada's 10 provinces saw their unemployment rates rise.
Despite market expectations, the Bank of Canada held off from cutting rates on Friday, but economists said the move was inevitable in the very near future.
Spence said Canada's stubbornly high unemployment rate means the Bank of Canada must ease interest rates further before signs of a lasting recovery in domestic demand are seen.

"The Bank must think about not just offsetting some of the Canadian dollar appreciation we've seen over the last month or so, but whether or not to chart an outright easing policy again," Spence said.
"Cut, cut, cut. Cut rates. It's quite clear you've got to cut rates," he added.
The September jump in the jobless rate was the second in four months. Unemployment soared to 10.0 percent in June, before easing to 9.8 percent in July and 9.4 percent in August.

"This report suggests to me that unless you see some evidence over the very near future that domestic demand is turning around, the Bank will also pursue probably another (cut of) 25 basis points," Spence said.
A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.

The central bank has already cut rates by two percentage points so far this year and by 4.25 percentage points since May 1995. The last seven rate cuts were independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve. The last cut, on Oct. 2, took the key overnight lending rate to a range of 3.50 to 4.0 percent and the Bank rate to 4.0 percent.
But the aggressive interest rate cutting seems to have done little to boost Canada's lagging economy.
"One gets the sense that the economy is just not living up to its potential," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers in Toronto.
He said the unemployment number for October would probably look even worse, due to the indirect impact of a continuing strike at General Motors' Canada unit.
"It's looking a little dismal out there and the economy just doesn't seem to be having that little bit of muster, that forward momentum," he said.
